A2.text:
Rashad is twenty-four. He finished university last year, but he does not have a job. Two companies decided to turn down his CV. He was very sad.

Then a big hotel in Baku invited him to an interview. There were five candidates for the job. The night before, Rashad practised with his sister, Leyla.

“What is your greatest strength?” Leyla asked.

“I am calm,” Rashad said.

“And your weakness?”

“I talk too fast when I am nervous.”

“Put your best foot forward,” Leyla said. “If something goes wrong, think on your feet. You can land a job this time.”

The next morning, Rashad put on his best suit. In the interview room, there were three managers. They asked about his qualification and his English. Then Rashad began his presentation on the computer.

Suddenly, the lights went off. There was no electricity! The computer screen was black.

The managers looked at each other. Rashad was nervous, but he had to think on his feet. He took a pen and a big piece of paper. He drew his ideas and explained them slowly and calmly.

When the lights came back, the managers were smiling.

“You stayed calm,” the director said. “In a hotel, that is very important.”

Two days later, the hotel called. The salary was good. First, there was a probation of three months. Rashad was very happy.

B1.text:
After graduating in tourism, Rashad spent six months sending out his CV. Two hotels decided to turn down his application without even meeting him, and a third never replied. So when the Caspian Grand invited him to interview for a guest relations job, he treated it like a final exam.

The night before, his sister Leyla played the role of a strict manager. “What's your biggest strength?”

“I stay calm under pressure.”

“Your biggest weakness?”

“When I'm nervous, I speak too quickly.”

“Then slow down,” Leyla said. “Put your best foot forward, smile, and you'll land a job this time. I can feel it.”

There were five candidates waiting in the lobby the next morning, all in dark suits, all pretending to read their phones. When Rashad's turn came, three managers asked about his qualification, his languages and a difficult guest he had once dealt with during his internship in Gabala. It was going well. Then he connected his laptop to start the presentation he had practised twenty times.

At the exact moment the first slide appeared, the building lost power. The screen died, the air conditioning stopped and the room went dark except for the grey light from the window.

Somebody laughed nervously. Rashad felt his heart racing, but he knew he had to think on his feet. He asked for a marker, walked to the whiteboard by the window and drew his ideas by hand — a simple map of a guest's first day at the hotel, with every moment where staff could make it special. He spoke slowly, exactly as Leyla had told him.

When the lights came back ten minutes later, nobody reached for the laptop.

“Most people would panic,” said the director. “You made a power cut look like part of the plan.”

The call came two days later. The salary was better than he had expected, with a three-month probation period. Rashad's first call was to Leyla.

B2.text:
By the time the Caspian Grand invited him for an interview, Rashad had been unemployed for six months and had developed a complicated relationship with his inbox. Two hotels had decided to turn down his CV without meeting him; a third had simply vanished into silence. A tourism degree, an internship in Gabala and fluent English, it seemed, were no longer remarkable — merely the minimum.

The evening before, his sister Leyla appointed herself his interviewer and adopted the expression of a woman who had rejected hundreds of applicants. “Your greatest strength?”

“I stay calm under pressure.”

“Your greatest weakness — and don't say perfectionism.”

“When I'm nervous, I talk far too fast.”

“Then breathe between sentences,” she said. “Put your best foot forward and stop apologising for existing. You will land a job this time.”

In the lobby next morning, five candidates in near-identical dark suits sat in rigid silence, pretending to read their phones. When his name was called, three managers worked steadily through his qualification, his languages and an awkward complaint he had once defused during his internship. He was beginning to relax. Then he plugged in his laptop to begin the presentation he had rehearsed until he could recite it in his sleep.

The first slide appeared — and the entire building lost power. The screen went black, the air conditioning sighed into silence, and the room was left in the dull grey light of a cloudy window.

Someone gave a nervous laugh. Rashad's pulse was pounding, but some calmer part of his brain observed that this was precisely the kind of moment a hotel employee is hired for. He would have to think on his feet. He asked for a marker, moved to the whiteboard nearest the window and sketched, freehand, a guest's first twenty-four hours at the Caspian Grand, marking every point at which a small gesture could turn a stay into a story. He spoke slowly, pausing exactly where Leyla had told him to.

When the electricity returned ten minutes later, nobody so much as glanced at the laptop.

“Most candidates would have frozen,” the director remarked. “You managed to make a power cut look intentional.”

The offer arrived two days later: a salary comfortably above his expectations, subject to a three-month probation. He dialled Leyla before he had finished reading the email.

podcast.title: My biggest weakness

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Have you ever had a job interview? Guess: what did Sam say when they asked about his biggest weakness?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is job interviews. Leyla, your cousin has a big interview tomorrow, right?
Yes, Murad. He wants to work for a big bank. He's so nervous that he practised with me all weekend.
Good. Did he prepare his CV?
Three times! But he's worried about the questions. Especially "What is your biggest weakness?"
[laugh] Oh, I have a terrible story about that question.
Tell us!
My first interview, at twenty-two. They asked about my biggest weakness, and I panicked. I said, "Chocolate."
[laugh] No!
Yes. Silence. Then one man laughed, and the woman wrote something in her notebook.
Did you get the job?
No. But I learned that you need to think on your feet — and prepare a real answer.
So what is a good answer?
Be honest, but show that you're working on it. For example: "I sometimes take on too much, so now I plan my week carefully."
And for strengths, Murad should give an example, not just say "I'm hard-working".
Exactly. Every candidate says that. A short true story is much better.
What about salary? Should he ask about money in the first interview?
Usually it's better to wait until they ask. But know your number before you go in.
Last year I had an offer from a big company, and I decided to turn down the job.
Really? Why?

The salary was good, but the hours were crazy. I wanted time for my life — and for this podcast! Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what advice would you give a friend who wants to land a job?
Mine: don't say chocolate. Good luck, Murad! See you next time!
Bye for now!
